rows.title: Asymptotic independence of descent sets and being an n-cycle
rows.record_statement:
For each $n$, let $[n-1]=\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let $\beta_n(I)$ denote the number of permutations in $S_n$ with descent set $I\subseteq[n-1]$, while $\beta^{\mathrm{cyc}}_n(I)$ denotes the number of $n$-cycles with descent set $I$. **Asymptotic independence conjecture.**

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{\varnothing \subsetneqq I \subsetneqq [n-1]} \left| \frac{n\, \beta^{\mathrm{cyc}}_n(I)}{\beta_n(I)} - 1\right| = 0.
$$

This asserts that, uniformly over all non-empty proper descent sets, having descent set $I$ and being an $n$-cycle are asymptotically independent, with the proportion of $n$-cycles tending to $1/n$ as it does among all permutations. The source presents this as a conjectural strengthening of the known asymptotic independence result for alternating permutations.
rows.source: Sergi Elizalde and Justin M. Troyka, “Exact and asymptotic enumeration of cyclic permutations according to descent set”, arXiv:1710.05103 (2019).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds. The source's own Theorem 3.1(c) writes n·β^cyc_n(I) as β_n(I) plus a signed sum, over the divisors d ≥ 2 of n, of the counts β_{n/d}(I/d) for the compressed descent sets, so everything reduces to showing that these smaller counts are negligible against β_n(I) uniformly in I. The source's bound for them is absolute and fails when β_n(I) is small. The new step is a counting inequality, β_n(I) ≥ (n^{2/3}/40)·β_{n/d}(I/d) for every divisor d ≥ 2 and every nonempty proper I: each permutation counted on the right is inflated into blocks and then modified either by swaps of disjoint free pairs (decoded by block rank sums) or by sliding a single letter along a long monotone run (at most four preimages), giving many distinct permutations with descent set I. With τ(n) ≤ 2√n this gives |n·β^cyc_n(I)/β_n(I) − 1| ≤ 80·n^{−1/6}. Lean defines β and β^cyc literally (permutations with exact descent set in one-line notation; cycles with full support), proves the counting inequality, the bound and the printed limit of the maximum, and takes Theorem 3.1(c) of the source as an explicit hypothesis.

rows.title: The strengthened 2-criticality conjecture for row-isotoped abelian 2-groups
rows.record_statement:
Let $L_s$ be the latin square of order $n=2^s$, and let $\alpha_{k,k'}$ be the row isotopism that interchanges rows $k$ and $k'$ and fixes every other row. Suppose that

$$
\left|k-k'\right|<3.
$$

**Strengthened 2-criticality conjecture.** The set $\operatorname{gcs}(\alpha_{k,k'}L_s)$ is 2-critical and strong, and completes top down to $\alpha_{k,k'}L_s$.

The theorem preceding this conjecture proves the claim under the additional hypothesis that $k$ and $k'$ lie among four consecutive indices beginning at a multiple of $4$. The authors expect that this stronger version remains true when that additional condition is weakened, but no resolution is given here.
rows.source: Carlo Hamalainen, “New 2–critical sets in the abelian 2–group”, arXiv:math/0612338 (2006).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds for every order 2^s and every pair of rows less than three apart, for the greedy order that the source describes in words and uses throughout (bottom row first, right to left). For each such swap the greedy critical set is given by explicit blank-cell masks written in binary across block boundaries; each clue is the lexicographically least cell of a private intercalate, which gives 2-criticality, and in each row the blanks are forced one at a time along an acyclic forcing graph, which gives strong completion and top-down completion. The source proved the case where both rows lie in an aligned block of four (its Theorem 5.1) and checked the rest by computer through order 32; the new cases are the swaps that cross a block boundary, of which the odd adjacent ones are easy and the two distance-two families carry the substance. Lean defines the square by bitwise exclusive or and proves it equal to the source's recursive square, defines the greedy algorithm with its uniqueness test over all Latin squares of the order, 2-criticality by private intercalates, strong completion and top-down completion by forced cells, and proves the three properties for all s and all such swaps. Lean also proves that with the source's displayed formula for the greedy order, which runs the other way, top-down completion fails at order four for the swap of rows 0 and 1.

rows.title: Lower bounds for the eigenvalue growth rate when p equals 2
rows.record_statement: Let $f(x)$ be a polynomial and let $\lambda=\lambda(f)$ be the associated growth rate. Two polynomials are **similar** when they are related by the transformations described in the paper. **Eigenvalue-bound conjecture.** When $p=2$, $\lambda\geq 3$. Moreover, $\lambda=3$ only for polynomials similar to $1+x$. If $p=2$ and $\lambda>3$, then $\lambda\geq 1+\sqrt{5}$; moreover, $\lambda=1+\sqrt{5}$ only if $f(x)$ is similar to $1+x+x^2$. These numerical bounds are inferred from computations and are presented as conjectural classifications of the first possible values of $\lambda$.
rows.source: Kevin Garbe, “Patterns In The Coefficients Of Powers Of Polynomials Over A Finite Field”, arXiv:1304.4635 (2013).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds for every polynomial over the field with two elements that has at least two nonzero terms: the growth rate λ of the number of nonzero coefficients in the first 2^k powers of f is at least 3, it equals 3 exactly when f is similar to 1+x, there is no value strictly between 3 and 1+√5, and it equals 1+√5 exactly when f is similar to 1+x+x^2. The bound λ ≥ 3 is short: after removing common powers every state of the section recursion has at least three children. The gap and the two classifications need more: multiplicities are projected modulo the direction of f, each three-way choice is deferred for a fixed number of steps, and states are weighted by (1+√5) to the number of pending choices; a count to any fixed depth cannot give 1+√5, as the polynomials 1+x+x^(2^m) show. For monomials the rate is 2 and for the zero polynomial it is 1, so the first sentence of the conjecture as printed fails there; the source's own tables and remarks concern non-monomials only. Lean defines the cumulative count, the growth rate as the limit of its k-th root along 2^k, and similarity as the equivalence relation generated by shift, dilation, reversal and powers, and proves the full statement for polynomials with at least two terms, as well as the values 2 and 1 in the degenerate cases.

rows.title: Rational spherical triangle measurement conjecture
rows.record_statement: Let a proper spherical triangle on the unit sphere have side lengths and area that are rational multiples of $\pi$, and let its measurement be the tuple $(E,a,b,c)$, with $a\le b\le c$. Define $\Lambda_1$ and $\Lambda_2$ as the sets of measurements given in the source. **Rational spherical triangle measurement conjecture.** The tuples in $\Lambda_1\cup\Lambda_2$ are the only measurements of proper rational spherical triangles. In particular, there are only finitely many measurements of proper rational spherical triangles with mutually distinct side lengths, namely, the seven measurements found by Little and Coxeter. This conjecture would classify all proper rational spherical triangles and implies that the mutually distinct-side cases are exactly the seven known examples.
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds: the rational solutions of L'Huilier's equation in the proper range are exactly the two-right-side family and the eight sporadic tuples of the source (one in Λ₁ and the seven of Λ₂), so by the source's Proposition 2.2 these are the only measurements of proper rational spherical triangles, and the seven with three distinct sides are the only such triangles. The proof is computer-assisted. In tangent coordinates the equation becomes a vanishing sum of 23 roots of unity. The new step is a line lemma: if the equation holds along a whole line of parameters through a proper point, the behaviour at the two ends of the segment forces the line into the two-right-side family. With the polygon inequality this gives a rank condition at every other solution, which shows that only the primes 2, 3, 5, 7 divide the common denominator and bounds their exponents, so the denominator divides 352,800 = 2⁵·3²·5²·7². An exact search over these denominators finishes the classification. Lean defines the solution set Ω₂ and the sets Λ₁, Λ₂ literally from the source and proves Ω₂ = Λ₁ ∪ Λ₂ with no hypotheses; the line lemma, the prime support, the exponent bounds and the whole finite search (replayed in the kernel in certified batches, with proofs that the batches cover every case) are inside Lean.

rows.title: Littlewood-admissibility conjecture for pairs with two interior zeros
rows.record_statement: Let $n\geq 1$, and let $(k,n)$ be a valid pair for Littlewood polynomials. A pair is **Littlewood-admissible** if some Littlewood polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $k$ zeros in the open unit disk and no zeros on the unit circle. **Littlewood-admissibility conjecture.** The pairs $(2,n)$ and $(n-2,n)$ with $n\equiv 1\pmod 6$ and $n\geq 13$ are the only non-trivial Littlewood-inadmissible pairs. Computations establish this classification for $n\leq31$, while the assertion for all larger degrees remains open.
rows.source: Kevin G. Hare and Jonas Jankauskas, “On Newman and Littlewood polynomials with prescribed number of zeros inside the unit disk”, arXiv:1910.13994 (2019).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds: for 1 ≤ k ≤ n−1, the pair (k, n) is inadmissible exactly when n ≥ 13, n ≡ 1 (mod 6) and k = 2 or k = n−2. There are two halves. Exclusion, for every such n (the source had it only up to n = 31, by exhaustive computation): a Littlewood polynomial with no zero on the circle and exactly two zeros inside is coprime to its reciprocal, so its Schur–Cohn form is nonsingular with exactly two negative directions; the tree of sign prefixes that survive this test is small and repeats with period 12, which is carried to every depth by stationary submatrices and 60 kernel vectors, and every completed word is excluded by an exact certificate. This half is computer-assisted: about 32,000 certificate cases, all checked in the Lean kernel together with proofs that they cover every case. Existence, for every other pair: most cases are theorems of the source; the remaining cases (even k ≥ 12 in two ranges) are filled by a new family of polynomials, whose zero counts are proved in Lean by a root-counting argument on arcs and a strict-dominance comparison. Lean defines Littlewood polynomials (all coefficients ±1), the count of zeros in the open disc with multiplicity, and admissibility literally, proves the Schur–Cohn root count from scratch, and proves the classification from five results of the source taken as explicit hypotheses.
